metadata.file_name: 84. Gong et al. (2023). Using process features to investigate scientific problem-solving in large-scale assessments.pdf
metadata.title: Using process features to investigate scientific problem-solving in large-scale assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NAEP 2018 science pilot tasks administered via technology-enhanced items (TEIs) and analyzes process features (preparation time, execution time, mean execution time per event) alongside rubric-based item scores. The manuscript does not report the use of NAEP sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analyses are based on nonparametric tests (Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and omnibus ANOVA/t-tests on process-feature distributions across score groups, the paper does not provide guidance on how to incorporate complex survey design weights into these inferential comparisons. For replication or extension with NAEP microdata, analysts should consult NAEP technical documentation to determine the appropriate student weight(s) and replicate weights for variance estimation, and then re-run the group-comparison tests under a weighted/replicate framework if population-representative inference is required.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are rubric-based item scores for specific NAEP science pilot TEIs (fair and exhaustive tasks), not PV-based cognitive achievement scales. Therefore, plausible values are not applicable to the outcome construction used here. The paper states that missing values were removed prior to analysis, so missing-data handling is addressed via case deletion rather than PV-based imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the 2018 NAEP science pilot tasks and selects four TEI testlets: two fair tests (grade 4 and grade 8 bands) and two exhaustive tests (grade 12 band). Analyses are conducted only on students whose process and response data were available for the respective testlets; the paper notes that data were missing due to early quit or data capture glitches and that the rightmost column in Table 1 records the number of students whose process and response data were used. Before analysis, the authors remove missing values for the process features (after which winsorization is applied to each process feature). No additional school-type or country subsampling is described beyond the grade-band/testlet selection inherent to the NAEP pilot tasks.

main_findings.dataset_used: NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Fair test 1, Grade 8, Earth/space science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Kruskal–Wallis: PT χ2=12.2, df=2, p<0.005; ET χ2=89.916, df=2, p<0.001; MET χ2=64.776, df=2, p<0.001. Omnibus ANOVA: PT F(2,1604)=5.943, p<0.005; ET F(2,1604)=51.7, p<0.001; MET F(2,1604)=38.93, p<0.001. Wilcoxon signed-rank: higher-score group had shorter ET; full-score group had shorter PT and MET than lowest-score group, but differences were not statistically significant when the partial-score group was included.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Fair test 1, Grade 8, Earth/space science) the study leveraged preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time (MET) to relate process features to rubric-based item score (1–3), finding that score groups differed significantly on all three temporal features (all Kruskal–Wallis p<0.005 and omnibus ANOVA p<0.005). This indicates that students’ planning and action-execution efficiency—captured by PT, ET, and MET—are strongly associated with successful control-of-variables performance, suggesting that process-informed scoring rubrics or feedback could target inefficient planning and hesitant execution stages.

main_findings.dataset_used: NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Fair test 2, Grade 4, Physical science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Kruskal–Wallis: PT χ2=7.824, df=2, p=0.02; ET χ2=78.111, df=2, p<0.001; MET χ2=6.600, df=2, p=0.037. Omnibus ANOVA: PT F(2,1987)=2.744, p=0.065 (non-significant); ET F(2,1987)=37.53, p<0.001; MET F(2,1987)=3.451, p=0.032. Wilcoxon signed-rank: higher-score group had shorter ET; full-score group had shorter PT and MET than lowest-score group, but differences were not statistically significant when the partial-score group was involved.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Fair test 2, Grade 4, Physical science) the study leveraged preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time (MET) to relate process features to rubric-based item score (1–3), finding significant group differences for ET and MET and marginal/non-significant evidence for PT depending on the test (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.02 for PT; ANOVA p=0.065). This indicates that execution efficiency (ET) and per-action efficiency (MET) are more consistently linked to correct control-of-variables reasoning than planning duration alone, suggesting instructional emphasis on reducing hesitation during action execution and improving efficient experimental setup.

main_findings.dataset_used: NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Exhaustive test 1, Grade 12, Life science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Kruskal–Wallis: PT χ2=133.57, df=3, p<0.001; ET χ2=498.49, df=3, p<0.001; MET χ2=258.97, df=3, p<0.001. Omnibus ANOVA: PT F(3,2721)=65.4, p<0.001; ET F(3,2721)=224.5, p<0.001; MET F(3,2721)=78.4, p<0.001. Wilcoxon signed-rank: full-score students had shorter PT and MET than lowest-score students; ET patterns differed such that full-score students were not uniformly shorter ET than all other groups (noted as a contrast with fair tests).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Exhaustive test 1, Grade 12, Life science) the study leveraged preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time (MET) to relate process features to rubric-based item score (1–4), finding significant differences across all score groups for PT, ET, and MET (all Kruskal–Wallis and omnibus ANOVA p<0.001). This indicates that exhaustive control-of-variables success is associated with both planning and execution efficiency, but with a task-dependent interpretation of total execution time, suggesting that process-aware feedback should distinguish between productive persistence (needed for exhaustive coverage) and inefficient execution.

main_findings.dataset_used: NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Exhaustive test 2, Grade 12, Earth/space science)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Kruskal–Wallis: PT χ2=10.317, df=3, p<0.017 (marginal); ET χ2=440.33, df=3, p<0.001; MET χ2=158.79, df=3, p<0.001. Omnibus ANOVA: PT F(3,2942)=3.094, p=0.026 (marginal); ET F(3,2942)=185.7, p<0.001; MET F(3,2942)=45.58, p<0.001. Wilcoxon signed-rank: full-score students had shorter PT and MET than other low-score students, but full-score students had longer ET than most other score students.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs (Exhaustive test 2, Grade 12, Earth/space science) the study leveraged preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time (MET) to relate process features to rubric-based item score (1–4), finding significant differences for ET and MET and weaker/marginal evidence for PT depending on the test (Kruskal–Wallis p<0.017; ANOVA p=0.026). This indicates that high performance in exhaustive testing reflects efficient per-action execution (MET) even when total execution time is longer, suggesting that scoring and feedback should reward sustained, goal-oriented exhaustive coverage rather than simply minimizing total time.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes NAEP 2018 science pilot TEIs using four scientific inquiry tasks (two fair tests for Grade 4 and Grade 8, and two exhaustive tests for Grade 12). Instead of training predictive ML models, the authors define three process features from event timestamps—preparation time (PT), execution time (ET), and mean execution time per answer-related event (MET)—and test whether these features differ across rubric-based score groups. Across all four tasks, Kruskal–Wallis and omnibus ANOVA results show statistically significant score-group differences for ET and MET, with PT showing stronger effects in fair tests and more mixed/marginal effects in exhaustive tasks. The paper also reports Wilcoxon signed-rank patterns: higher scores generally correspond to shorter ET in fair tests, while exhaustive tasks show longer ET for full-score students but shorter PT and MET. Limitations include the absence of survey-weight reporting and the use of group-comparison tests rather than a predictive evaluation with cross-validation, so results support relatedness rather than causal or out-of-sample predictive claims.
